children: By Kirk Maltais

Wheat for December delivery fell 1.4% to $7.16 1/4 a bushel on the Chicago Board of Trade Tuesday, with trading stagnant as traders await the result of Thursday's planned summit between the U.S. and China.
Corn for December delivery fell 1.2% to $5.36 1/4 a bushel.
Soybeans for November fell 0.2% to $13.25 a bushel.
HIGHLIGHTS
Waiting for the Summit: CBOT grain futures settled mixed, with traders treading cautiously ahead of the U.S.-China summit.

"Grain markets are basically in pause mode as traders await trade details from the meeting on Thursday between Xi Jinping and President Trump in Washington," said Brian Grete of Commstock Investments. He added that the net long positions held by fund traders are another reason why traders are reluctant to push grains higher ahead of the summit for fear of a large liquidation event if the meeting results in a negative sentiment.

Addressing the World: On top of the Trump-Xi summit, traders were also tentative as President Trump spoke in front of the United Nations on Tuesday. Traders didn't derive much from the speech, and the large long positions held in grains by fund traders means that it will take a lot to move prices even higher.
"It looks like the easy money is over in the grains," said Charlie Sernatinger of Marex in a note.
INSIGHT

State of Turmoil: Ongoing conflicts around the globe continue to be a factor that is supporting grain futures in the longer term, said analysts with Rabobank in a note. The firm's Agri Commodity Markets Research group said that fighting in the Black Sea and Middle East is feeding the need for grains traders to add "risk premium" to grain futures.
"The biggest threats to agricultural commodity markets currently remain the Black Sea situation, disruption around the Strait of Hormuz, and El Niño," the firm said.

Setting the Tone: Higher energy and food prices are likely to keep inflation measures above the Fed's 2% target until March, Goldman Sachs' David Mericle writes. Crude prices are easing this week, but remain elevated. Mericle notes that refined products "have risen disproportionately," adding pressure on consumer prices.

He expects the upward pressure on energy and food price to "keep headline PCE inflation near 3.5% through year-end before a drop-off to 2.5% in March 2027 and 2.0% in May as base effects kick in," he said.

Outpacing the Prior Year: The USDA said the pace of early harvesting in the U.S. is exceeding that of this time last year, as well as the five-year average pace. The government says corn is 13% harvested, while soybeans are 12% complete, with corn 3 points ahead of this time last year, while soybeans are 4 points ahead of last year's pace.
Rainfall this week may slow down harvest progress, said Michael Cordonnier of Soybean and Corn Advisor in a note, although the Central Plains should dry out later this week.
AHEAD
General Mills Inc. is scheduled to release its first-quarter 2027 earnings report at 7 a.m. EDT Wednesday.
The EIA is due to release its Weekly Petroleum Status Update Report at 10:30 a.m. EDT Wednesday.
The USDA is scheduled to release its weekly export sales report at 8:30 a.m. EDT Thursday.
The USDA is due to release its quarterly hogs and pigs report at 3 p.m. EDT Thursday.
Paulo Trevisani contributed to this article.
